exercises.title: Style a Bio Page Using Element, Class, and ID Selectors
exercises.problemHtml:
Every real stylesheet starts with the same decision: which selector reaches which element. A <h1> tag selector touches every heading of that level on the page, a class like .highlight can be reused on any number of unrelated elements, and an id like #tagline is a promise that only one element on the page will ever carry it. Mixing these up is one of the most common beginner mistakes: writing a class selector to do an id selector's job invites duplicate ids later, and reaching for an id when a reusable class was the right tool creates a stylesheet full of one-off rules that cannot be reused anywhere else on the site.

You are given a short bio page with a heading, three paragraphs (two sharing a class, one carrying a unique id), and an empty stylesheet with TODO markers for each selector type. Complete the CSS so it satisfies exactly these requirements.

  • 1. Every <h1> element is styled with a type selector: color #1a1a1a and font-family: Georgia, serif.
  • 2. Every <p> element is styled with a type selector: color #333333, font-family: Arial, sans-serif, and line-height: 1.5.
  • 3. Both paragraphs carrying class="highlight" get background-color: #fff3cd and font-weight: bold from a single shared class selector, not two separate rules.
  • 4. Only the paragraph carrying id="tagline" gets font-style: italic and color: #0066cc, from a single id selector.
  • 5. No inline style attribute may be added to the HTML.

The HTML file is complete and must not be edited; only styles.css has TODO comments for you to fill in, one per selector type.

A complete index.html with an

exercises.outputSpec: styles.css defines exactly four rules — a type selector for h1, a type selector for p, a class selector for .highlight, and an id selector for #tagline — producing the colors, fonts, weights, and background described in the requirements, with no inline styles anywhere.
exercises.constraints: Do not edit index.html. Do not add inline style attributes. Do not write two separate rules for the two .highlight paragraphs — one class selector must cover both. Do not use an id selector for anything except #tagline. Do not use !important.

examplesJson.input: class="highlight" applied to two unrelated paragraphs
examplesJson.output: Both paragraphs render with a pale yellow background (#fff3cd) and bold text, from one .highlight rule.
examplesJson.explanation: A class selector matches every element carrying that class, however many there are on the page, so one rule is enough — writing it twice would be redundant.

examplesJson.input: id="tagline" used on a single paragraph
examplesJson.output: Only that one paragraph renders italic in blue (#0066cc); the other paragraphs keep the default p color and are not italic.
examplesJson.explanation: Ids are meant to be unique per page — reusing the same id on two elements is invalid HTML — so an id selector always targets at most one real match.

The single

examplesJson.explanation: A type selector matches every element of that tag name and nothing else, which is why it is the right tool for a page-wide default like heading color.

hintsJson: Start with the two type selectors — h1 and p — since they set the baseline every other rule builds on top of.
A class selector starts with a dot and can match many elements at once; write .highlight { } exactly once, not once per element.
An id selector starts with a hash and should only ever match the single element that carries that id; write #tagline { } for the italic blue line.
Check your final file has exactly four rules: h1, p, .highlight, #tagline — no more, no fewer, and no inline style attributes in the HTML.

exercises.solutionExplanationHtml:
The two type selectors, h1 and p, set the baseline every paragraph and heading inherits before anything more specific is applied. The class selector .highlight then layers a background and bold weight on top of that baseline for both paragraphs that carry the class, without touching their color or font — which is why they still read in the same dark gray as every other paragraph. The id selector #tagline does the same layering for exactly one element.

The common trap here is reaching for two separate rules to style the two .highlight paragraphs, usually by accident when a learner treats CSS like inline styling applied one element at a time. A single class selector already matches every element with that class on the page, so writing it twice is redundant and, if the two copies ever drift apart, becomes a real bug. The same discipline applies to #tagline: because ids are meant to be unique, there is never a reason to write an id selector more than once per id.

exercises.title: Style a Navigation Menu with Descendant Selectors and Hover States
concepts: scoping selectors to avoid unwanted matches
exercises.problemHtml:
Navigation links almost never live alone on a page — they sit inside a <nav> next to a footer link, a sidebar link, or article links that must look completely different. A bare a { } type selector cannot tell those apart; it repaints every link on the page the same way, which is exactly why real stylesheets scope link styles with a descendant selector like .main-nav a instead. The same scoping problem applies to removing bullet markers: ul { list-style: none; } would strip bullets from every list on the page, including ones that were never meant to look like a menu.

You are given a page with a <nav class="main-nav"> containing a three-item link list, and a separate <footer> with its own unrelated link. Style only the navigation menu.

  • 1. Remove the bullet markers and default spacing from the list inside the nav using the descendant selector .main-nav ul, setting list-style: none, margin: 0, and padding: 0.
  • 2. Make the list items inside the nav sit in a horizontal row using .main-nav li with display: inline-block and margin-right: 4px.
  • 3. Style every link inside the nav using the descendant selector .main-nav a: text-decoration: none, color: #222222, display: inline-block, and padding: 8px 12px.
  • 4. Add a hover state using .main-nav a:hover that switches to text-decoration: underline and color: #0066cc.
  • 5. The footer's link must keep the browser's default blue, underlined appearance — do not write a bare a selector anywhere in the file, since that would repaint the footer link too.

The scaffold's HTML is complete; styles.css has one TODO comment per rule described above.
exercises.inputSpec: A complete index.html with <nav class="main-nav"> wrapping a <ul> of 3 links, and a separate <footer> with one unrelated <a>. styles.css is empty except for TODO comments marking the four rules to write.
exercises.outputSpec: styles.css contains four rules, all scoped under .main-nav (.main-nav ul, .main-nav li, .main-nav a, .main-nav a:hover), producing a horizontal, unbulleted menu whose links underline and turn blue on hover, while the footer link keeps its default browser styling untouched.
exercises.constraints: Do not write a bare a, ul, or li type selector anywhere — every rule must be scoped with the .main-nav descendant selector. No JavaScript. No inline style attributes. Do not add, remove, or reorder any HTML elements.

examplesJson.input: .main-nav a:hover applied while pointing at one of the three menu links
examplesJson.output: That link underlines and turns #0066cc; the other two nav links and the footer link are unaffected.
examplesJson.explanation: A descendant selector combined with :hover only matches an anchor nested inside .main-nav while the cursor is directly over it.

examplesJson.input: a bare a { color: red; } rule added anywhere in the file
examplesJson.output: The footer's Privacy Policy link would also turn red, which the requirements forbid.
examplesJson.explanation: A type selector with no scoping class matches every anchor on the page, including ones outside the intended component.

examplesJson.output: Only the <ul> inside .main-nav loses its bullets; any other list elsewhere on the site keeps its default markers.
examplesJson.explanation: Scoping the selector to .main-nav is what prevents the rule from leaking to unrelated lists on the same page.

hintsJson: A descendant selector is just two selectors separated by a space — .main-nav a means any a anywhere inside an element with class main-nav, however deeply nested.
Scope every rule the same way: .main-nav ul, .main-nav li, .main-nav a — never write the bare tag alone, or the footer link inherits it too.
:hover is a pseudo-class attached directly to a selector with no space: .main-nav a:hover, not .main-nav a :hover.

Finish with: .main-nav ul { list-style: none; margin: 0; padding: 0; } .main-nav li { display: inline-block; margin-right: 4px; } .main-nav a { text-decoration: none; color: #222222; padding: 8px 12px; display: inline-block; } .main-nav a:hover { text-decoration: underline; color: #0066cc; }

exercises.solutionExplanationHtml:
Every rule is scoped with the descendant selector .main-nav ... so it can only ever match elements nested inside the nav, which is what keeps the footer's link completely untouched even though both are <a> tags. .main-nav li { display: inline-block; } is what turns three stacked list items into a horizontal row, and .main-nav a { display: inline-block; } is what lets padding actually add clickable space around each link instead of being partially ignored the way it would be on a plain inline element.

The common trap is writing a bare a { } or ul { } rule out of habit, which silently repaints every link and list on the page — invisible here with only one footer link, but a real bug the moment the page grows a sidebar or article links. :hover must also be attached directly to the selector with no space (.main-nav a:hover), since a space before it would make it a separate, non-matching descendant selector instead of a pseudo-class on the anchor itself.

exercises.title: Resolve a Style Conflict Using the Cascade and Specificity
concepts: combining an id selector with a class selector
exercises.problemHtml:
When two CSS rules target the same element and set the same property, the browser does not average them or apply both — exactly one wins, decided by a fixed set of rules called the cascade. Source order is the simplest of those rules: the rule written later in the file wins when specificity is tied. Specificity is the more powerful rule: it scores every selector by how many ids, classes, and type selectors it contains, and the higher score wins regardless of source order. Understanding this is what separates a developer who can predict what a stylesheet will render from one who reaches for !important the moment two rules disagree, which only postpones the same problem to the next conflict.

You are given a stylesheet with three existing rules that already conflict on the color property for one paragraph, plus one plain paragraph with no class or id. Add exactly one new rule that wins the conflict without editing the existing rules and without using !important.

  • 1. Do not edit or remove the existing p, .message, or #notice rules already present in styles.css.
  • 2. Do not use !important anywhere in the file.
  • 3. Do not introduce a second id selector.
  • 4. Add exactly one new rule, placed after the existing rules, whose selector combines the id notice with the class warning (for example #notice.warning) so it outscores the existing #notice rule.
  • 5. That new rule sets color: #ffffff and background-color: #b30000 on the element with id="notice".
  • 6. The plain paragraph with no class or id must still render using only the existing p rule — color #333333, no background — completely unaffected by your new rule.

The scaffold's HTML and the three existing CSS rules are complete and must not change; only the final TODO rule is yours to write.
exercises.inputSpec:
index.html has two paragraphs: a plain

and

. styles.css already contains three complete rules — p, .message, #notice — that conflict on color, plus one TODO comment where your new rule goes.
exercises.outputSpec: The notice paragraph renders with white text (#ffffff) on a dark red background (#b30000); the plain paragraph is unaffected and still shows the existing p rule's color (#333333) with no background.
exercises.constraints: Do not edit the three existing rules. No !important anywhere. No second id selector. The new selector must combine #notice with a class to outrank #notice alone. Exactly one new rule, placed after the existing ones.

examplesJson.input: only the three existing rules p, .message, #notice are present (no new rule yet)
examplesJson.output: The notice paragraph renders green (#006600) from the #notice rule, since an id selector outranks both the type selector p and the class selector .message.
examplesJson.explanation: Specificity compares ids first, then classes, then type selectors — one id already beats any number of type or class selectors alone.

examplesJson.output: The notice paragraph now renders white text on a dark red background, overriding the plain #notice rule's green.
examplesJson.explanation: #notice.warning still counts one id, but also counts one class, so column by column it scores higher than #notice alone, even though both target the same id.

examplesJson.input: two class selectors of equal specificity, .message and .warning, both setting color, with no id involved
examplesJson.output: Whichever one is written later in the stylesheet wins, since their specificity scores are tied.
examplesJson.explanation: Source order is only the tiebreaker used when specificity is exactly equal — it never overrides a real specificity difference.

hintsJson: Specificity is scored as three counts: id selectors, class or pseudo-class selectors, and type selectors — compare them in that order, left to right, before ever guessing.
#notice alone scores one id and nothing else; to beat it without adding another id, add a class to the same selector so it scores one id and one class.
#notice.warning has no space between the id and the class, meaning both must be true on the same element — the notice paragraph already carries both, so it matches.
Write #notice.warning { color: #ffffff; background-color: #b30000; } after the three existing rules; do not touch p, .message, or #notice.

exercises.solutionExplanationHtml:
Specificity is compared as three separate counts — ids, then classes or pseudo-classes, then type selectors — read left to right like digits, never added together into one score. #notice alone scores one id, which already beats p (one type) and .message (one class) regardless of where those three rules sit in the file. Adding !important would work but is a trap: it does not fix the underlying conflict, it just adds a new, harder-to-override layer that causes worse conflicts later.

The fix is #notice.warning, which still counts as one id, but now also counts one class, so column by column it outranks #notice alone even though both selectors target the same id. This is the key idea: specificity is not "ids always win no matter what" — a more specific selector referencing the same id always beats a less specific one referencing it, with zero source-order ambiguity and zero !important. The plain paragraph never matches any of the class or id rules, so it is untouched by the whole conflict.

  Combo[Id plus class hash notice dot warning scores one one zero]

  Class --> Id
  Id --> Combo
  Combo --> Winner[Highest specificity wins the conflict]

exercises.title: Style an Article's Typography with Relative Units and Hex Colors
concepts: border width as a fixed (non-scaling) unit
exercises.problemHtml:
Font sizes set in fixed pixels ignore a reader's own browser settings entirely — someone who increased their default text size because of low vision gets no benefit from a page built entirely in px, because 16px always renders as sixteen actual pixels no matter what. A size set in rem is relative to the root element's font size instead, so it scales automatically with the reader's preferences, which is why real stylesheets use rem for font sizes and reserve px for things that should never scale, like a hairline border.

You are given a complete article page — a title, a byline, two paragraphs, and a pull quote — and an empty stylesheet with one TODO comment per element group. Style its typography using relative units and hex colors throughout.

  • 1. body: font-family: Georgia, 'Times New Roman', serif and color: #222222.
  • 2. h1: font-size: 2.5rem, font-weight: 700, line-height: 1.2, color: #111111.
  • 3. p (the type selector, covering both body paragraphs): font-size: 1rem and line-height: 1.6.
  • 4. .byline: font-size: 0.875rem, color: #767676, letter-spacing: 0.02em, text-transform: uppercase.
  • 5. blockquote: font-size: 1.25rem, font-style: italic, color: #444444, border-left: 4px solid #cccccc, padding-left: 1rem.
  • 6. Every font-size declaration must use rem, never px — the one exception is the blockquote's 4px border width, which stays in px because a border should not scale with text.
  • 7. Every color value must be a 6-digit hex code, never a named color like gray or black.

The HTML is complete and unedited; only styles.css's five TODO comments are yours to fill in.
exercises.inputSpec: A complete index.html article with h1, p.byline, two plain p paragraphs, and one blockquote, linked to an empty styles.css with five TODO comments, one per element or class group.
exercises.outputSpec: styles.css defines five rules (body, h1, p, .byline, blockquote) using rem for every font-size and hex codes for every color, matching the exact values in the requirements.
exercises.constraints: No font-size in px. No named colors (e.g. gray, black, red) — hex only. Do not edit index.html. No inline style attributes. The blockquote's border-left width stays in px.

examplesJson.input: root font-size is the browser default of 16px, and h1 { font-size: 2.5rem; }
examplesJson.output: The h1 renders at 40px, since 2.5rem is always 2.5 times the root element's font-size.
examplesJson.explanation: rem is relative to the root <html> element's font-size, not the parent element's, which is what makes it predictable no matter how deeply an element is nested.

examplesJson.input: a reader increases their browser's default text size from 16px to 20px
examplesJson.output: Every rem-based size on the page grows proportionally, including the heading and body text, while a px-based size would have stayed frozen at its original pixel value.
examplesJson.explanation: This is the core reason rem is preferred for font sizes in real stylesheets: it respects the reader's own accessibility settings automatically.

hintsJson: Start from the outside in: body sets the shared font-family and base text color every other rule inherits from.
rem always scales from the root <html> element's font-size, never from a parent element — that is what makes it predictable across nested content.
letter-spacing and text-transform are what make .byline read as a small, spaced-out label instead of a normal sentence.
Finish blockquote with a 4px solid left border in a light gray hex color, 1rem of left padding to separate the border from the text, and italic 1.25rem text in a darker gray than the border.

exercises.solutionExplanationHtml:
Every font-size in the solution is written in rem, which is always relative to the root <html> element's font-size rather than to whatever element it happens to be nested inside — that is what makes a 2.5rem heading resize predictably if a reader changes their browser's default text size, something a 40px heading would never do. The blockquote's 4px border is the deliberate exception: a border is a fixed visual line, not body text, so it should stay a constant pixel width regardless of font scaling.

The common trap is mixing named colors like gray into an otherwise hex-based stylesheet; named colors are imprecise (there is no easy way to tell gray from darkgray at a glance) and make a codebase harder to search. Hex codes like #767676 are exact and greppable across a whole project. .byline's text-transform: uppercase paired with a small positive letter-spacing is the standard pattern for a muted metadata label — uppercase alone often reads as visually cramped without the added spacing.

exercises.title: Build a Three-Card Stack Using the Box Model and box-sizing: border-box
concepts: the box model (content, padding, border, margin)
box-sizing: border-box versus the content-box default
percentage width inside a fixed-width container
exercises.problemHtml:
A width declared in CSS does not automatically include a box's padding or border — by default, width: 100% plus 16px of padding and a 1px border on every side renders wider than the containing box, because padding and border are added on top of the declared width, not absorbed into it. Inside a fixed-width column this overflow is exactly why a card can visually poke out past its container even though every number in the stylesheet looks correct. The fix is box-sizing: border-box, which redefines width to mean the box's full outer size, padding and border included.

You are given a narrow 320px column holding three stacked plan cards, each with a heading and a paragraph, and an empty stylesheet with TODO markers. Style it so every card fits the column exactly, with consistent spacing.

  • 1. .card-list: width: 320px, background-color: #f2f2f2, padding: 10px.
  • 2. Every .card: box-sizing: border-box, width: 100%, padding: 16px, border: 1px solid #cccccc, border-radius: 4px, background-color: #ffffff, margin-bottom: 12px.
  • 3. Every .card h3: margin: 0 0 8px 0, color: #111111.
  • 4. Every .card p: margin: 0, color: #555555, line-height: 1.4.
  • 5. The box-sizing: border-box declaration on .card is mandatory, not optional: without it, a card with width: 100% plus 16px of padding and a 1px border on each side would render wider than .card-list's content area and visually overflow past the column's edge.
  • 6. Do not set a fixed pixel width on .card — it must stay 100% so it always matches whatever width .card-list happens to have.

The HTML is a complete, unedited three-card list; styles.css has four TODO comments, one per selector group above.
exercises.inputSpec: index.html has a .card-list div containing three .card divs, each with an h3 and a p, fully written with real plan names and descriptions. styles.css is empty except for four TODO comments.
exercises.outputSpec: Three cards, each exactly matching .card-list's 320px width including padding and border (thanks to box-sizing: border-box), stacked with 12px of gap between them inside a light gray 320px column, matching the exact colors, padding, and border values in the requirements.
exercises.constraints: Do not set a fixed px width on .card — it must be 100%. box-sizing: border-box is required on .card. Do not edit index.html. No inline style attributes.

examplesJson.input: content-box default (no box-sizing rule), card with width 100% plus 16px padding plus 1px border
examplesJson.output: The card renders wider than .card-list's content box and visually overflows past its rounded corners.
examplesJson.explanation: The default box-sizing: content-box adds padding and border on top of the declared width instead of including them inside it.

examplesJson.input: box-sizing: border-box added to the same card
examplesJson.output: The card's total rendered width becomes exactly 100% of .card-list's content area, padding and border included, with no overflow.
examplesJson.explanation: border-box redefines width to mean the full outer box, so padding and border are subtracted from the available space instead of added on top.

hintsJson: Style the outer column first — .card-list's fixed width and light gray background give you a visual container to check the cards against.
By default, width only covers the content area; padding and border are added outside of it. box-sizing: border-box changes width to mean the full box instead.
Give every .card box-sizing: border-box, width: 100%, and its padding/border/radius/background together — the order inside the rule does not matter, but all of them are required.

Finish with margin-bottom: 12px on .card for spacing between cards, and margin: 0 on .card h3/.card p so the browser's default heading and paragraph margins do not add extra unpredictable gaps inside each card.

exercises.solutionExplanationHtml:
The key decision is box-sizing: border-box on .card. Without it, the browser's default content-box model treats width: 100% as the size of the content area alone, then adds 16px of padding and 1px of border on every side on top of that — a card that looks like it should fit its 320px column instead renders wider and visually overflows. With border-box, width: 100% means the padding and border are subtracted from the available space instead of added to it, so the rendered box always matches its container exactly.

The other common trap is leaving the browser's default heading and paragraph margins in place inside each card — <h3> and <p> both carry built-in top and bottom margins that would add inconsistent extra space above the heading and around the paragraph, on top of the card's own 16px padding. Resetting them with margin: 0 (and a small deliberate 8px bottom margin on the heading) keeps the internal spacing entirely predictable and controlled by the stylesheet, not by browser defaults.

exercises.title: Capstone: Style a Complete Profile Card with the Box Model and a Positioned Status Badge
concepts: combining class selectors across a whole component
position: relative and position: absolute together
exercises.problemHtml:
A profile card is one of the most common real components on the web, and building one correctly means combining nearly everything from this module at once: class selectors to scope every rule to the card, the box model with box-sizing: border-box so the card and its button never overflow their declared sizes, and position: relative paired with position: absolute to pin a small status dot to the exact corner of a circular avatar without it drifting away when the layout changes. Each piece depends on the one before it: the badge only stays glued to the avatar's corner because the avatar's wrapper establishes the positioning context it is measured against.

You are given a complete profile card — an avatar with a status dot, a name, a title, a bio, and a follow button — and an empty stylesheet with one TODO comment per group of related elements. Style the whole component.

  • 1. .profile-card: box-sizing: border-box, width: 280px, padding: 24px, border: 1px solid #e0e0e0, border-radius: 12px, background-color: #ffffff, text-align: center, margin: 0 auto.
  • 2. .avatar-wrap: position: relative, width: 80px, height: 80px, margin: 0 auto 16px.
  • 3. .avatar image: fills its wrapper (width: 100%, height: 100%), circular via border-radius: 50%, object-fit: cover, display: block.
  • 4. .status-dot: position: absolute, pinned bottom: 2px; right: 2px against the avatar's corner, width: 14px, height: 14px, background-color: #2ecc71, a 2px solid #ffffff border, border-radius: 50%.
  • 5. .name: margin: 0 0 4px 0, font-size: 1.25rem, color: #111111.
  • 6. .title: margin: 0 0 12px 0, font-size: 0.875rem, color: #767676, text-transform: uppercase, letter-spacing: 0.03em.
  • 7. .bio: margin: 0 0 20px 0, font-size: 0.9375rem, color: #444444, line-height: 1.5.
  • 8. .follow-btn: box-sizing: border-box, padding: 10px 24px, border: none, border-radius: 6px, background-color: #111111, color: #ffffff, font-weight: 600, cursor: pointer.
  • 9. .follow-btn:hover: background-color: #333333, with no other property changed, so the button never shifts size on hover.
  • 10. Only class selectors may be used — no bare button, img, or h2 type selectors anywhere in the file.

The HTML is complete and unedited; styles.css has eight TODO comments, one per rule group above.
exercises.inputSpec: A complete index.html with .profile-card wrapping .avatar-wrap (containing .avatar img and .status-dot span), .name h2, .title p, .bio p, and .follow-btn button. styles.css is empty except for eight TODO comments.
exercises.outputSpec: A centered 280px card with rounded corners and a border, a circular 80px avatar with a small green status dot pinned to its bottom-right corner, centered name/title/bio text, and a dark rounded follow button that darkens on hover without changing size — matching every value in the requirements exactly.
exercises.constraints: Use only class selectors — no bare button, img, or h2 type selectors. box-sizing: border-box required on .profile-card and .follow-btn. The hover state may only change background-color, nothing else. Do not edit index.html. No inline style attributes, no JavaScript.

examplesJson.output: The .status-dot, being position: absolute, positions itself against the nearest positioned ancestor instead — typically the whole page — and drifts away from the avatar entirely.
examplesJson.explanation: Absolute positioning always measures its offsets from the nearest ancestor that has a position other than static; forgetting to set one is a silent bug, not an error.

examplesJson.input: .follow-btn:hover changing padding instead of only background-color
examplesJson.output: The button visibly grows or shrinks on hover, shifting the layout of anything positioned near it.
examplesJson.explanation: Hover states should avoid changing box-model properties like padding, border, or width, since that causes a visible layout shift every time the cursor moves over the element.

examplesJson.output: An 80px circular avatar with a small white-bordered green dot glued to its bottom-right corner, centered name, title, and bio text, and a dark Follow button that only darkens on hover.
examplesJson.explanation: Every piece — box model, centering, circular avatar, absolute-positioned badge, and hover state — combines into one coherent, reusable component.

hintsJson: Build outer to inner: .profile-card's box model and centering first, then .avatar-wrap, then the avatar image and status dot inside it, then the text block, then the button.

position: absolute always measures its bottom/right/top/left against the nearest ancestor that is not position: static — that is exactly why .avatar-wrap needs position: relative even though it has no offset of its own.
A circle from a square box only needs one property: border-radius: 50% — apply it to both .avatar and .status-dot, and add object-fit: cover on the avatar so a non-square photo does not distort.

Finish .follow-btn and its :hover state together: the base rule sets every box-model and color property, and the hover rule changes only background-color — nothing else — so the button never resizes when the user points at it.

exercises.solutionExplanationHtml:
The status dot's position depends entirely on one earlier decision: .avatar-wrap has position: relative, which makes it the positioning context that .status-dot's position: absolute offsets are measured against. Without that one line, the dot would still be absolutely positioned, but relative to the nearest positioned ancestor above it in the whole document — typically nothing, which means the page itself — and it would jump toward the corner of the browser window instead of the corner of the avatar. This is the single most common trap with absolute positioning: it always works relative to something, and forgetting to declare that something is a silent bug, not an error.

Two box-sizing: border-box declarations, on .profile-card and .follow-btn, exist for the same reason as in the earlier box-model exercise: both elements combine an explicit size with padding and a border, and without border-box both would render larger than their declared dimensions. The hover state deliberately changes only background-color — changing padding or border on hover is a common beginner shortcut that causes the whole button, and anything below it, to visibly shift position every time the cursor moves over it.
